A beginner can first practise shaking or striking it by hand like a handbell, then apply most handbell techniques; holding six chimes at once is hard, and striking with a mallet is not allowed. In classroom teaching each student takes a particular note and no one plays all the time, and through this they learn theory, each player's responsibility and teamwork.

Most handbell techniques can be applied to the handchime, though some are harder or impossible. Its notes are written as diamond-shaped noteheads, unlike the oval noteheads of the handbell.

The source notes that it began as a training tool for future handbell players, and that because it is cheaper, lighter and more durable than a handbell it suits school groups, church youth choirs and groups of older people. Handbell ensembles often keep handchimes, and some handbell pieces call for handbells and handchimes together, or alternate between them from section to section. Handchimes are also used for music teaching in the classroom.

Its design derives from a bamboo instrument of Southeast Asia, refined by several American inventors; in 1982 Malmark made the first modern handchimes. In 2018 there were three makers in the United States: Malmark, Schulmerich and Suzuki.
